curation: Observed r5questions plus source-read false-premise development controls; not a new unseen test.

questions.question: What separate purchase amounts did the FOMC announce on March 18, 2009 for agency mortgage-backed securities, agency debt, and longer-term Treasuries, and which amounts were additions or totals?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: To provide greater support to mortgage lending and housing markets, the Committee decided today to increase the size of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet further by purchasing up to an additional $750 billion of agency mortgage-backed securities, bringing its total purchases of these securities to up to $1.25 trillion this year, and to increase its purchases of agency debt this year by up to $100 billion to a total of up to $200 billion. Moreover, to help improve conditions in private credit markets, the Committee decided to purchase up to $300 billion of longer-term Treasury securities over the next six months.
goldEvidence.rationale: The two sentences name each instrument, distinguish additional purchases from annual totals for MBS and agency debt, and state the separate Treasury amount and horizon.

economicChecks: Agency MBS: up to an additional $750 billion, bringing total purchases to up to $1.25 trillion in 2009.
Agency debt: up to an additional $100 billion, bringing the annual total to up to $200 billion.
Longer-term Treasuries: up to $300 billion over the next six months; do not assign the MBS or agency-debt amount to Treasuries.
Keep the up-to limits; these are announced purchase decisions, not evidence that the amounts were ultimately purchased.

questions.question: In its November 3, 2010 announcement, how much more in longer-term Treasury securities did the FOMC intend to buy, by when, and at roughly what monthly pace?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: In addition, the Committee intends to purchase a further $600 billion of longer-term Treasury securities by the end of the second quarter of 2011, a pace of about $75 billion per month.
goldEvidence.rationale: A single sentence supplies the additional Treasury amount, completion horizon, and approximate monthly pace.

economicChecks: Identify further purchases of longer-term Treasury securities, not agency MBS.
State $600 billion by the end of Q2 2011 at about $75 billion per month.
Preserve intends and about; do not describe the sentence as a verified realized total.

questions.question: How was the maturity-extension operation announced by the FOMC on September 21, 2011 structured in terms of purchase amount, maturities, offsetting sales, and deadline?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: The Committee intends to purchase, by the end of June 2012, $400 billion of Treasury securities with remaining maturities of 6 years to 30 years and to sell an equal amount of Treasury securities with remaining maturities of 3 years or less.
goldEvidence.rationale: This sentence gives all four requested operational elements, including the offsetting sales that distinguish maturity extension from unoffset net purchases.

economicChecks: Purchase $400 billion of Treasuries with remaining maturities of 6–30 years by end-June 2012.
Sell an equal amount of Treasuries with remaining maturities of 3 years or less.
Do not present the $400 billion as an unoffset increase in total securities holdings.

questions.question: What additional asset purchases, including the instrument and monthly amount, did the FOMC agree to on September 13, 2012?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: To support a stronger economic recovery and to help ensure that inflation, over time, is at the rate most consistent with its dual mandate, the Committee agreed today to increase policy accommodation by purchasing additional agency mortgage-backed securities at a pace of $40 billion per month.
goldEvidence.rationale: The sentence identifies the new purchase instrument and its monthly pace without conflating it with the combined effect of other ongoing operations.

economicChecks: Additional agency mortgage-backed securities at $40 billion per month.
Do not replace this instrument-specific $40 billion pace with the approximately $85 billion combined monthly increase described elsewhere.
This is an asset-purchase decision; do not report a policy-rate increase.

questions.question: Under the purchase changes announced on December 18, 2013, how were monthly agency MBS and longer-term Treasury purchases to change beginning in January?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: Beginning in January, the Committee will add to its holdings of agency mortgage-backed securities at a pace of $35 billion per month rather than $40 billion per month, and will add to its holdings of longer-term Treasury securities at a pace of $40 billion per month rather than $45 billion per month.
goldEvidence.rationale: The sentence separately gives the new and preceding monthly pace for each of the two instruments and states when the change starts.

economicChecks: Beginning in January 2014: agency MBS $35 billion rather than $40 billion per month.
Longer-term Treasuries $40 billion rather than $45 billion per month.
This reduces the pace of additions to holdings; it does not say the Fed sold these securities or immediately reduced its stock of holdings.

questions.question: On October 29, 2014, what did the FOMC decide about its asset-purchase program, reinvestment policy, and federal funds target range?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: Accordingly, the Committee decided to conclude its asset purchase program this month. The Committee is maintaining its existing policy of reinvesting principal payments from its holdings of agency debt and agency mortgage-backed securities in agency mortgage-backed securities and of rolling over maturing Treasury securities at auction. This policy, by keeping the Committee's holdings of longer-term securities at sizable levels, should help maintain accommodative financial conditions. To support continued progress toward maximum employment and price stability, the Committee today reaffirmed its view that the current 0 to 1/4 percent target range for the federal funds rate remains appropriate.
goldEvidence.rationale: The contiguous passage covers the conclusion of the purchase program, continuing reinvestment and rollovers, and the unchanged target range.

economicChecks: Conclude the asset-purchase program in October 2014 while maintaining principal reinvestment and Treasury rollovers.
The federal funds target range remains 0–0.25%.
Ending purchases is not a rate increase and is not an announcement that all securities holdings would run off.

questions.question: When the FOMC raised rates on December 16, 2015, what new target range did it choose, what inflation confidence did it express, and how did it describe the policy stance after the increase?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: The Committee judges that there has been considerable improvement in labor market conditions this year, and it is reasonably confident that inflation will rise, over the medium term, to its 2 percent objective. Given the economic outlook, and recognizing the time it takes for policy actions to affect future economic outcomes, the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 1/4 to 1/2 percent. The stance of monetary policy remains accommodative after this increase, thereby supporting further improvement in labor market conditions and a return to 2 percent inflation.
goldEvidence.rationale: The three sentences directly pair the rate decision with the stated inflation confidence and the continuing accommodative stance.

economicChecks: Raise the target range to 0.25–0.50%.
Reasonably confident that inflation will rise to 2% over the medium term is a forward-looking assessment, not evidence that inflation was already 2%.
Policy was described as remaining accommodative after the increase.

questions.question: What federal funds target range did the FOMC choose on July 31, 2019, why did it lower rates, and how did it change the timing for ending the reduction in its securities holdings?

goldEvidence.rationale: This sentence provides the new range and the stated global-outlook and inflation motivations.

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: The Committee will conclude the reduction of its aggregate securities holdings in the System Open Market Account in August, two months earlier than previously indicated.
goldEvidence.rationale: This separate sentence supplies the revised end date and the two-month timing comparison for securities-holdings reduction.

economicChecks: Lower the federal funds target range to 2.00–2.25%, citing global developments and muted inflation pressures.
Conclude securities-holdings reduction in August 2019, two months earlier than previously indicated.
Earlier describes timing; it does not by itself specify a smaller monthly runoff amount or the start of new net asset purchases.

questions.question: In its March 15, 2020 response to the coronavirus disruption, what target range did the FOMC set and what minimum increases in Treasury and agency MBS holdings did it announce for the coming months?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: In light of these developments, the Committee decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate to 0 to 1/4 percent.
goldEvidence.rationale: This is the rate decision and resulting range.

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: To support the smooth functioning of markets for Treasury securities and agency mortgage-backed securities that are central to the flow of credit to households and businesses, over coming months the Committee will increase its holdings of Treasury securities by at least $500 billion and its holdings of agency mortgage-backed securities by at least $200 billion.
goldEvidence.rationale: This sentence supplies the distinct minimum increases for the two instruments, the coming-months horizon, and the market-functioning purpose.

economicChecks: Lower the federal funds target range to 0–0.25%.
Increase Treasury holdings by at least $500 billion and agency MBS holdings by at least $200 billion over coming months.

Distinguish the rate decision from securities purchases and do not substitute later March 2020 unlimited-purchase wording for this dated announcement.

questions.question: What target range did the FOMC adopt on June 15, 2022, and what did it say about further rate increases and the reduction of securities holdings?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: In support of these goals, the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 1‑1/2 to 1-3/4 percent and anticipates that ongoing increases in the target range will be appropriate. In addition, the Committee will continue reducing its holdings of Treasury securities and agency debt and agency mortgage-backed securities, as described in the Plans for Reducing the Size of the Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet that were issued in May.
goldEvidence.rationale: The two sentences provide the new range, the conditional outlook for ongoing rate increases, and continuing balance-sheet reduction.

The Committee anticipated that ongoing increases would be appropriate; this is guidance rather than a realized schedule of later increases.
Continue reducing Treasury, agency debt, and agency MBS holdings; do not describe this as restarting asset purchases.

questions.question: At its July 31, 2024 meeting, what federal funds target range did the FOMC retain, and what inflation-related confidence did it require before expecting a rate reduction to be appropriate?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: In support of its goals, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent. In considering any adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks. The Committee does not expect it will be appropriate to reduce the target range until it has gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent.
goldEvidence.rationale: The passage couples the unchanged range with the explicit confidence condition for a future reduction.

economicChecks: Maintain 5.25–5.50%.
A reduction was not expected to be appropriate until greater confidence that inflation was moving sustainably toward 2%.
Do not convert this condition into an announced date or guarantee of a cut.

questions.question: What inflation confidence did the FOMC express on September 18, 2024, what rate reduction and new target range did it choose, and how did Michelle Bowman’s preferred action differ?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: The Committee has gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent, and judges that the risks to achieving its employment and inflation goals are roughly in balance. The economic outlook is uncertain, and the Committee is attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate. In light of the progress on inflation and the balance of risks, the Committee decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/2 percentage point to 4-3/4 to 5 percent.
goldEvidence.rationale: The passage gives the confidence assessment, balance of risks, and majority decision including both size and resulting range.

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: Voting against this action was Michelle W. Bowman, who preferred to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.
goldEvidence.rationale: The dissent sentence identifies Bowman and her preferred quarter-point reduction.

economicChecks: The majority cut by 0.50 percentage point to 4.75–5.00%.
Bowman dissented in favor of a smaller 0.25 percentage-point cut, not a rate hold or increase.
Greater confidence in sustainable progress toward 2% is not a claim that inflation had already reached 2%.

questions.question: What downside inflation risk did the FOMC identify in its January 28, 2009 statement, and how certain was that assessment?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: Moreover, the Committee sees some risk that inflation could persist for a time below rates that best foster economic growth and price stability in the longer term.

questions.question: According to the July 2017 FOMC meeting minutes released on August 16, how did the Committee expect inflation to differ between the near term and the medium term?

Attribute this expectation to Committee members in the policy-action discussion, not to a separate staff forecast.
The meeting was July 26, 2017; the minutes were published August 16, 2017.

questions.question: In the FOMC minutes released on April 7, 2021, what did the staff forecast production bottlenecks and supply constraints would do to inflation that year, and for how long?

Staff forecast in minutes of the March 17, 2021 meeting, published April 7, 2021; do not treat the meeting date as the publication date.

questions.question: What did the OECD’s March 17, 2025 interim outlook project for US core inflation in 2026, and what bilateral tariff assumption accompanied those projections?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: Core inflation is now projected to remain above central bank targets in many countries in 2026, including the United States. These projections are based on an assumption that bilateral tariffs between Canada and the United States and between Mexico and the United States are raised by an additional 25 percentage points on almost all merchandise imports from April.

US core inflation was projected to remain above target in 2026; do not label this headline inflation or realized 2026 data.

An assumed tariff increase is not evidence that the assumed policy was enacted or that it alone explains the projection.

questions.question: In its June 6, 2024 outlook, what did the ECB identify as sustaining domestic price pressures, and how long was inflation likely to stay above target?

Inflation was likely to remain above target well into 2025, relative to the June 2024 publication.
Preserve likely and the outlook horizon; do not state an observed 2025 outcome or import a forecast for a different country.

questions.question: For Türkiye in the OECD outlook published on June 30, 2017, what was the consumer-inflation situation and how fast was disinflation projected to proceed?

Slow disinflation means a projected slowing in inflation, not a prediction of a fall in the consumer price level.

questions.question: In its June 8, 2022 outlook for Türkiye, what level did the OECD expect consumer inflation to exceed that year, and which monetary-policy and price conditions did it cite?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: Accommodative monetary policy coupled with high commodity and food prices will keep consumer inflation above 70% in 2022.
goldEvidence.rationale: The original forecast supplies the above-70% threshold, the 2022 horizon, and both policy and price conditions.

The cited combination is accommodative monetary policy with high commodity and food prices.
The source uses will in a dated outlook; describe it as that forecast rather than as verified realized annual inflation.

questions.question: What federal funds target range did the FOMC set in its December 16, 2008 statement, and what reasons did that statement give?
questions.rationale: The requested primary statement predates this bounded source collection. Fed document publication coverage begins January 14, 2009; the 801 timeline notes begin January 28, 2009. Later passages may mention 2008, but that cannot substitute for the requested December 2008 statement or establish its complete reasons.
economicChecks: Abstain from providing the requested December 2008 statement answer as source-supported.
Do not substitute the January 2009 target range, external knowledge, or a later retrospective mention for the missing primary statement.

questions.question: What reasons did the Bank of England itself give in its July 2014 Monetary Policy Committee minutes for keeping Bank Rate unchanged?
questions.rationale: The Fed corpus contains Fed and OECD documents; all 18 GBR timeline notes are attributed to the OECD, and no timeline source institution is the Bank of England. A request for the Bank of England’s own July 2014 minutes is therefore outside this collection, even if OECD UK assessments discuss monetary policy.
economicChecks: Abstain from claiming to quote or summarize the Bank of England’s own minutes.
Do not relabel OECD UK commentary or a Fed statement as a Bank of England primary source.

questions.question: What inflation outlook did Brazil’s central bank give in its September 2024 Copom statement?
questions.rationale: The complete 801-note timeline inventory contains zero BRA-country notes and its institution inventory has no Banco Central do Brasil. The other eligible source collection consists of Fed passages. This is a request for a Brazil-specific central-bank statement outside the indexed country and institution scope, not a claim that Brazil is never mentioned incidentally.
economicChecks: Abstain from a Brazil-specific Copom answer using this collection.
Do not transfer the Fed, ECB, or Türkiye inflation outlook to Brazil or supply an uncited answer from prior knowledge.

questions.question: Why did Michelle Bowman prefer a three-quarter-percentage-point rate cut in the September 18, 2024 FOMC statement?
questions.rationale: The original September 18, 2024 statement explicitly says Bowman preferred a one-quarter-percentage-point cut. The question’s three-quarter-point premise contradicts the source; the statement also does not provide a fuller personal rationale for that invented preference. The control is established by the read dissent sentence, not by an unverified search absence.
economicChecks: Reject the unsupported 0.75-percentage-point preference.
The source supports a 0.25-percentage-point preferred cut; it does not supply a reason for the invented larger cut.
Do not fabricate an explanation or infer that Bowman preferred a rate hold.

questions.question: In their 2010 assessments, what inflation path did the OECD describe for Hungary and the FOMC describe for the United States, including any target, horizon or economic conditions attached to each?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: Inflation is expected to be below the central bank’s 3% inflation target by the end of 2011.
goldEvidence.rationale: The OECD projected inflation below Hungary’s 3% target by end-2011.

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: Measures of underlying inflation have trended lower in recent quarters and, with substantial resource slack continuing to restrain cost pressures and longer-term inflation expectations stable, inflation is likely to be subdued for some time.
goldEvidence.rationale: The FOMC expected subdued US inflation, with resource slack and stable longer-term expectations.

economicChecks: Attribute the Hungary forecast to the OECD on 26 May 2010 and the US outlook to the FOMC on 10 August 2010; these are different issuers and publication months.
Keep Hungary’s end-2011 horizon and 3% target separate from the US description of subdued inflation for some time.
Describe the US slack and expectations conditions; do not invent a US numerical forecast or infer a cross-country inflation gap.

questions.question: Compare what the OECD’s November 2011 outlook said about inflation prospects in Chile and Slovakia and the qualifications attached to each economy.

goldEvidence.rationale: Slovakia’s lower-inflation outlook was linked to real household income and less pronounced regulated-price increases.

economicChecks: Preserve Chile’s 3% (+/–1) target range and the stated projection-period horizon; the excerpt does not give an exact end date.
For Slovakia, describe lower inflation and the projected household-income benefit, including the regulated-price explanation.
Do not turn Slovakia’s qualitative outlook into a numerical inflation forecast or treat the Chilean target as a forecast point.

questions.question: What did the IMF’s 2012 assessments project for headline inflation in Latvia and Lithuania, and what condition accompanied Latvia’s projection?

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: Headline inflation should fall to around 2.6 percent in 2012, provided there are no shocks to world energy or food prices.

goldEvidence.expectedQuote: Headline inflation expected to fall to around 3 percent in 2012.
goldEvidence.rationale: The Lithuania passage gives its separate approximate 2012 headline-inflation projection.

Retain Latvia’s proviso that there are no shocks to world energy or food prices.
Identify the publication dates as 16 May and 14 June 2012; do not copy 2015 URL migration dates into the economic chronology.

Attribute Iceland’s stated monetary tightening and appreciation to that economy; do not invent target values or exact inflation rates.

questions.question: What inflation paths did the OECD’s first 2014 outlook issue project for Belgium and Canada, and how did it relate those paths to economic slack?
